$$

Consider the modified Lotka-Volterra model, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators.

questions.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity is given by

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

In our case, the equation describing the dynamics of the prey is given by

$$
{x}^{′}=3.2x(1-0.05x)-1.6xy
$$

where 

- the $3.2x(1-0.05x)$ term defines the growth, and

- the $-1.6xy$ term defines the decay due to interaction with predators.

In the case of the complete absence of predators, we have $y=0,$ and this equation becomes

$$
{x}^{′}=3.2x(1-0.05x).
$$

General solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3.2x(1-0.05x)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,20\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=20.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the maximum capacity.

Therefore, the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators is $20.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=3x(1-0.25x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-2y+xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. The equilibria of the model are the following:

$(0,0),\,(${{field-1}}$,0),\,(${{field-2}}$,${{field-3}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3x(1-0.25x)-xy=0 \\ -2y+xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2y+xy & =0 \\ y(-2+x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3x(1-0.25x)-x(0) & =0 \\ 3x(0.25x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(4,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2)(1-0.25(2))-(2)y & =0 \\ 3-2y & =0 \\ y & =1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2,1.5).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(4,0),\,(2,1.5).
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=x(1-0.2x)-2xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(1-0.2x)-2xy)=1-0.4x-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x(1-0.2x)-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+xy)=-3+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}1-0.4x-2y & -2x \\ y & -3+x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}1-0.4(0)-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 0 & -3+0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=8x(1-0.75x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-4y+4xy\end{aligned} $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[1,\,2]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=8x(1-0.75x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-4y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8x(1-0.75x)-xy)=8-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8x(1-0.75x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4y+4xy)=-4+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}8-12x-y & -x \\ 4y & -4+4x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}8-12(1)-(2) & -(1) \\ 4(2) & -4+4(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 \\ 8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -1 \\ 8 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(-\lambda )-8(-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since both eigenvalues are real and negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x(1-2x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-2x)-xy)=4-16x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+3xy)=-3+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}4-16x-y & -x \\ 3y & -3+3x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}4-16(0)-0 & -0 \\ 3(0) & -3+3(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=3x(1-2x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-3y+4xy\end{aligned} $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.5,\,0]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=3x(1-2x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=3-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+4xy)=-3+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}3-12x-y & -x \\ 4y & -3+4x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}3-12(0.5)-0 & -0.5 \\ 4(0) & -3+4(0.5)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -0.5 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Carrying Capacity for the Prey
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=6x(1-0.1x)-3xy \\ {y}^{′}=-7y+5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the modified Lotka-Volterra model, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity is given by

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

In our case, the equation describing the dynamics of the prey is given by

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x) - 3xy
$$

where 

- the $6x(1-0.1x)$ term defines the growth, and

- the $-3xy$ term defines the decay due to interaction with predators.

In the case of the complete absence of predators, we have $y = 0,$ and this equation becomes

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x).
$$

General solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x(1-0.1x)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,10\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=10.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the maximum capacity.

Therefore, the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators is $10.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Equilibrium Points of the Modified Lotka-Volterra System
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-0.2x)-4xy \\ {y}^{′}=-6y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the equilibria of the model.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4xy=0 \\ -6y+3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4x(0) & =0 \\ 5x(0.2x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(5,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5(2)(1-0.2(2))-(4)(2)y & =0 \\ 10(1-0.4)-8y & =0 \\ 10(0.6)-8y & =0 \\ 6-8y & =0 \\ y & =0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2, 0.75).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
(5, 0), \qquad
(2, 0.75).
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.5, \, 2.5]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=5x(1-x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x(1-x)-xy)=5-10x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/52a848e561f814865aa10f5196bdf756a7f3a83a65e2cb5442f6df17709f2a1d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/cbdbf12c92fcce1f2fedcf11402643b8bbe75bf08b48de3f0d36a0a0bb814d2d.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/29b4d10f386df1ad331ef73a88986089cf90d566128ee8abc69dcad53392ed3b.svg)

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2.5-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2.5-\lambda )(-\lambda )-5(-0.5) & =0 \\ \lambda (2.5+\lambda )+2.5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2.5\lambda +2.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2} = -1.25 \pm 0.25\sqrt{15}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an asymptotically stable spiral sink.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Predator Extinction Case
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x(1-2x)-3xy \\ {y}^{′}=-5y+4xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.5, \, 0]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-2x)-3xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-5y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-2x)-3xy)=4-16x-3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-2x)-3xy)=-3x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-5y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-5y+4xy)=-5+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/6282a23eb5bd51c399548652efe32b63b2b69b661776c99b2aa2168a2d11366c.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/902cae135690e7001927c07cfd15e72805cb65d7ba645659e0c30f19e2016226.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -4$ and $\lambda_2=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is an asymptotically stable sink.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Predator Extinction Case

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with **carrying capacity** is given by 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, 

- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and

- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.

The only difference from the Lotka–Volterra model is the factor $(1-hx)$ in the prey equation. Notice that if $h=0,$ we get the standard model:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

In our modified version of the model, the *intrinsic growth* of prey is given by the $ax(1-hx)$ term. Now, if there are no predators ($y=0$), then 

$$
x' = ax(1-hx).
$$

Recall that general solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,\frac{1}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{h}.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the *carrying capacity* (the limit the number of prey is approaching as $t$ goes to infinity).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/8b7a6d12af77f6c2d2e6d3596e71a51a3d697a5c28e9f9c64c5675a01df812d5.png)

tutorials.name: Equilibrium Points
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, for the Lotka–Volterra model 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy=0 \\ -cy+dxy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

tutorials.name: Local Behavior Near the Origin
tutorials.problem:
Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model.

tutorials.title: Local Behavior Near the Origin
tutorials.content:
Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model.

tutorials.name: Local Behavior Near the Nonzero Equilibria
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

Notice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when 

$$
h < \dfrac{d}{c},
$$

which guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.

We now evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)

Because we are considering the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that

$$
\dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Analyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

tutorials.title: Local Behavior Near the Nonzero Equilibria
tutorials.content:
Recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

Notice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when 

$$
h < \dfrac{d}{c},
$$

which guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.

We now evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)

Because we are considering the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that

$$
\dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Analyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/a7673170825344e1831f2ba01ce4c20f10091380ff4e116f3b6bd9e7666e51aa.png)

tutorials.name: A Worked Example for the Equilibrium on the x-Axis
tutorials.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x(1-0.25x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-2y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

We'll evaluate its Jacobian at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[4, \, 0]^T$ that lies on the $x$-axis.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-0.25x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=4-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/0bd1edc4527b82bebf84d38f8d4a79b65062d6b38c5fa4c84b7509acaa547f42.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/30463f939876ccbee7cf77f8fdc80fb4e8a27fe0ad5af22cd51e1be3433a3af5.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/fc40e7e568705e08b70e0dedae710b2e8514837491730ae12a90bed764261f97.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = 10$ and $\lambda_2=-4$. Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

tutorials.title: A Worked Example for the Equilibrium on the x-Axis
tutorials.content:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x(1-0.25x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-2y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

We'll evaluate its Jacobian at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[4, \, 0]^T$ that lies on the $x$-axis.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-0.25x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=4-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/0bd1edc4527b82bebf84d38f8d4a79b65062d6b38c5fa4c84b7509acaa547f42.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/30463f939876ccbee7cf77f8fdc80fb4e8a27fe0ad5af22cd51e1be3433a3af5.svg) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/fc40e7e568705e08b70e0dedae710b2e8514837491730ae12a90bed764261f97.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = 10$ and $\lambda_2=-4$. Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Let's now see an example with the equilibrium that lies in the first quadrant (the third equilibrium).

tutorials.name: Predator Extinction Case
tutorials.problem:
Again, recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

We have already considered the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ which guarantees that the third equilibrium will lie in the first quadrant. Let's now consider the remaining cases.

- When $h = \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium coincides with the second one. So, we have only two equilibria:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right) = \left(\dfrac{c}{d}, 0\right)
$$

- When $h > \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium is in the fourth quadrant (its $y$-coordinate is negative). So, we have only two equilibria that make sense in the context of the model:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

Hence, we get only two equilibria. 

The trajectories near the origin remain similar. However, the equilibrium at

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

will be an *asymptotically stable sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h \geq \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/b94beebb63bc1312d56f655e48b3bc7cdb1b9badc5cdacd6b88b073c5055adc9.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14157408/assets/cd60f32a5daff3c805b097d121814d19e04781ed1bcfead989cde82db674e5d9.png)

Eventually, the *predators go extinct* while the prey approaches the carrying capacity of the system.

Let's see a concrete example.
